As the shock front traverses a structure, a pressure is imparted to the roof slab and side walls equal to the incident shock pressure at a given time at any specified point reduced by a negative drag pressure. The portion of the surface loaded at a particular time is dependent upon the magnitude of the shock front incident pressure, the location of the shock front, and the wavelength $(L_{w}\mathrm{a n d}L_{w}\bar{})$ of the positive and negative shock pressure pulses. Values for $L_{w}$ and $L_{w}^{-}$ can be determined from Figure 2-15 (+) and Figure 2-16 (+) for the typical case of a surface burst.

To determine accurately the overall loading on a surface, a step-by-step analysis of the shock wave propagation across the surface should be made. This analysis includes an integration of the pressures at various points (Figure 2-195a (+)) on the surface and at various times to determine the equivalent uniform incident pressure acting on a span L as a function of time (Figure 2-195b (+)). Since the regions of maximum stress in the component vary along the span length as the shock front traverses the surface,,the component should be designed with constant cross sectional properties along the span length to ensure it will respond as intended when it is designed using the equivalent uniform pressure.

As the shock wave traverses the roof or side walls, the peak value of the incident pressure decays and the wave length increases. As illustrated in Figure 2-195b $(\pm)$ _,the equivalent uniform pressure will increase linearly from time $t_{f},$ when the blast wave reaches the beginning of the component (point f), to time $t_{d}$ when the peak equivalent uniform pressure is reached. The equivalent uniform pressure will then decrease to zero when the blast load at point b in Figure 2-195a (+) on the component decreases to zero.

To simplify the calculations, the equivalent uniform pressure has been expressed as a function of the blast wave parameters at point f in Figure 2-195a (+). The equivalent load factor $C_{E}$ , the rise time, and duration of the equivalent uniform pressure are obtained from Figure 2-196 (+), Figure 2-197 (+), and Figure 2-198 (+), respectively, as a function of the wave length-span ratio $L_{w f}/L$
